question: In a large city littering is always a problem. The state anti-littering statute forbids throwing trash and other matter from any vehicle onto the public roads. John is stopped and given a $50 ticket. Can he succeed with a defense that he didn't know what his children were doing and that he had no criminal intent to break any laws?
options: No, because his criminal intent is clearly established by the circumstances of the events.
No, because ignorance of the law is not a valid defense.
No, because as the parent, John is legally responsible for the actions of his minor children.
No, because the law considers the vehicle as a single entity, and therefore everyone inside is responsible.
Yes, because John can argue that the littering was accidental and not intentional.
Yes, because John was not the one who directly committed the offense.
Yes, because he didn't know what his children were doing in the back seat and he had not participated in the violation nor did he know that they did it or were going to do it.
No, because this is likely a strict liability law that does not provide for defenses based on mental state.
Yes, because the police have no way of proving who in the car threw the garbage out the window.
Yes, because the law does not explicitly state that the driver of the vehicle is responsible for the actions of the passengers.
gold: No, because this is likely a strict liability law that does not provide for defenses based on mental state.

question: Four years ago the owner of a shopping center leased a store in the center for a 10-year term to a pharmacistfor use as a drugstore. The leaseincluded provisions that described the shopping center by metes and bounds; identified the entrances, parkingareas, signs, and other common facilities of the shopping center; and set out a covenant that the owner wouldnot lease any part of the shopping center to another drugstore. Last year the owner purchased a parcel of land immediately adjacent to the shopping center. That parcel wasimproved with a building that, at the time of the owner's purchase and for ten years earlier, was occupied inpart by a food supermarket and in part by a discount drugstore, under leases which the prior owner assignedto the owner. The owner reconstructed the common facilities of both shopping centers to integrate them and combine themso that, to the public, the two centers appeared as a larger single development. The pharmacist learned that the lease of the discount drugstore was about to expire and that the ownerplanned to enter into a new lease of the same space with the discount drugstore. The pharmacist protested the proposed new lease, but the owner declared his intention to go forward with it. The pharmacist brought an appropriate action to enjoin the new lease to the discount drugstore as a violationof the covenant in the pharmacist's lease. If the court finds for the owner, what will be the likely reason?
options: The covenant does not apply to the owner's actions as he did not directly lease the space to another drugstore but bought a property which already had a lease with a drugstore.
The owner's purchase and integration of the adjacent parcel of land effectively nullifies the existing covenant.
The drugstore use on the adjacent parcel was in existence when the owner and the pharmacist firstentered into the lease.
The discount drugstore on the adjacent parcel is not considered a 'new' lease, but a continuation of an existing one.
A covenant cannot restrict the use of land not owned by the covenantor when the covenant wascreated.
The owner has the right to lease any part of his property to any business, regardless of existing leases.
The pharmacist did not adequately express his concerns to the owner before initiating legal action.
A covenant that attempts to restrict competition is invalid as against public policy even if it runs with theland.
The covenant in the pharmacist's lease can be fairly construed as to apply only to the original shoppingcenter premises.
The covenant is not applicable as the shopping centers were considered separate entities at the time of the lease agreement.

succeed, because the contract requires the carpenter to deliver the storm windows within a specified time frame.
not succeed, because the carpenter's performance would be excused by the unforeseeable act of God.

succeed, because the carpenter had completed the storm windows but failed to deliver them.

question: A homeowner buys a new leaf blower and is so impressed with its power that he gets carried away and blows large amounts of his work onto the next door neighbor's yard. In addition to leaves, he also blew large amounts of pest-infested plant debris onto the neighbor's property. The material has accumulated into large, unsightly piles and caused damage to the neighbor's healthy plants. He has to pay workers to haul the material away and he incurs expenses to replace infected perennials. The neighbor sues for the tort of trespass. The homeowner files a motion to dismiss because the neighbor cannot prove that homeowner acted with an intent to trespass or to do harm. Will the court grant the motion to dismiss?
options: Yes, because the homeowner expected the wind to carry the debris away and did not think that it would accumulate on the neighbor's property.
No, because the homeowner's actions resulted in a direct invasion of the neighbor's property.
Yes, because the debris was not intentionally directed at the neighbor's property.
Yes, because the homeowner was not aware of the pest-infested debris.
No, because the neighbor was able to prove financial loss from the damage caused.
No, because trespass is based on an intentional act of entering the land or sending something onto the land, and the actor does not have to intend harm to be liable for the tort.
Yes, because the homeowner had no practical way of controlling where the material went and he acted without malice or ill will.
Yes, because the homeowner did not physically enter the neighbor's property.
No, because the infected debris constituted an abnormally dangerous condition and homeowner could be held strictly liable for the trespass.
No, because the act of blowing debris onto the neighbor's land constitutes a trespass regardless of intent.
gold: No, because trespass is based on an intentional act of entering the land or sending something onto the land, and the actor does not have to intend harm to be liable for the tort.
